nations.name: Baka
nations.lands: forests of eastern and southern Cameroon, northern Gabon, and neighbouring parts of the Republic of the Congo and Central African Republic

facts.text: In Gabon, the Baka are one of nine Indigenous forest peoples, alongside the Babongo, Bakoya and others, each with its own language and culture.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Gabon chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In 2025 a Batouri workshop run by the association ASBABUK and Cameroon's forestry ministry focused on fully recognizing Baka as rightful partners in managing forest resources.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Cameroon
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Sengwer
nations.lands: Cherangany Hills and Embobut Forest in Kenya's western highlands

facts.text: Sengwer society is organized around clans, each with its own roles, and elders guide decisions and teach younger generations.
Sengwer knowledge includes sustainable ways of hunting, gathering, beekeeping and caring for forest resources, which helps conserve biodiversity.

nations.name: Kabyles
nations.lands: Kabylia in north-eastern Algeria, with a large community in France

facts.text: Taqbaylit, the Kabyle language, is one of three Amazigh languages taught from bachelor's level to doctorate at Inalco in Paris.

source.title: Kabyle (Berber)
source.publisher: Inalco (Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales)

facts.text: Kabyles make up around half of Algeria's Amazigh population, centred on Kabylia in the north-east.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Algeria chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Mozabite
nations.lands: the M'Zab valley around Ghardaïa in the Algerian Sahara

facts.text: UNESCO credits the M'Zab with an ingenious system for capturing and sharing water which, with its palm groves, makes life work in a semi-desert.
The M'Zab valley habitat, built in the tenth century by the Ibadites around five ksour (fortified towns), survives intact and is UNESCO World Heritage.

nations.name: BaAka
nations.lands: forests between the Oubangui and Sangha rivers, in south-western Central African Republic and northern Republic of the Congo

facts.text: Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas credits BaAka knowledge of the forest as central to its research, conservation and tourism work.
The Central African Republic, home to many BaAka communities, ratified ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous peoples in 2010, the first African state to do so.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2021: Central African Republic
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Seminole Nation of Oklahoma
also: The Great Seminole Nation of Oklahoma
nations.lands: Wewoka and Seminole County, Oklahoma, United States; earlier homelands in Florida

facts.text: The Seminole Nation of Oklahoma is made up of fourteen bands, and its General Council seats two representatives from each band rather than from districts.

source.title: The Great Seminole Nation of Oklahoma: Written Testimony to the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs
source.publisher: Seminole Nation of Oklahoma, via U.S. Senate Committee on Indian Affairs

facts.text: The Seminole Nation Language Program works to maintain, revitalize and carry forward the language and traditional ways of the Seminole people.

nations.name: Rappahannock Indian Tribe
nations.lands: the lower Rappahannock and Mattaponi river watersheds in Virginia, as described by the Tribe's environmental department

facts.text: The Tribe's environmental department says it coordinates the Return to the River youth program.

source.title: Department Of Environmental Services | Rappahannock Indian Tribe

facts.text: The Tribe dates its incorporation to 1921 as part of efforts to strengthen its government and seek recognition.

nations.name: United Cherokee AniYunWiYa Nation
nations.lands: Guntersville, Alabama

facts.text: A January 2020 post describes a Word of the Month practice series, with a new calendar of practice planned for February.
In January 2020, the Nation announced a plan to highlight enrolled citizens' crafted items in its public posts.

source.title: Attention: United Cherokee AniYunWiYa Nation Artisans - UCAN

nations.name: Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe
nations.lands: Akwesasne, on the St. Lawrence River in northern New York, United States; the wider Akwesasne community extends into Canada

facts.text: The Saint Regis Mohawk Tribal Council is made up of three Chiefs, three Sub-Chiefs and a Tribal Clerk, with elections scheduled each year and set terms of office.

source.title: History of Tribal Government | SRMT - NSN

facts.text: The Tribe describes its original homeland as northeastern New York State, reaching into southern Canada and Vermont.

source.title: History of Tribal Government | SRMT - NSN

nations.name: Coharie Tribe
nations.lands: Harnett and Sampson Counties in southeastern North Carolina, where the Tribe locates its present community

facts.text: The Tribe's government page describes the Coharie Intra-Tribal Council as representing Harnett and Sampson Counties.
The Tribe's history locates the present Coharie population in North Carolina's Harnett and Sampson Counties.

nations.name: Seneca Nation
nations.lands: Allegany, Cattaraugus and Oil Spring territories in Western New York, United States

facts.text: The Seneca Nation governs itself under a constitution established in 1848, with a 16-member Tribal Council drawn equally from the Cattaraugus and Allegany territories.

source.title: Seneca Nation of Indians - Official Website

facts.text: The Seneca Nation runs a language immersion program so students can hold conversations in Onöndowa’ga:’ Gawë:nö’, the Seneca language, alongside classes and online learning.

nations.name: Cherokee Nation
nations.lands: Tahlequah and a 14-county reservation area in Oklahoma, United States; original homelands in the Southeast

facts.text: Cherokee Nation governs through legislative, executive and judicial branches and serves people across a 14-county reservation area.
Written Cherokee uses a syllabary, not an alphabet, with 85 distinct characters; Cherokee Nation teaches it through an immersion school and a master-apprentice program.

nations.name: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians
nations.lands: The Qualla Boundary in western North Carolina, United States, beside the Great Smoky Mountains

facts.text: As a sovereign nation, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians makes its own laws, holds its own elections and runs its own government and institutions.

source.title: Home - Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians

facts.text: The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians makes its home on the 56,000-acre Qualla Boundary, next to Great Smoky Mountains National Park.

source.title: NC Tribal Communities | NC DOA
source.publisher: North Carolina Department of Administration, Commission of Indian Affairs

nations.name: Seminole Tribe of Florida
nations.lands: Big Cypress, Brighton, Fort Pierce, Hollywood, Immokalee and Tampa reservations in Florida, United States

facts.text: The Tribal Council, with a Chairman, a Vice-Chairman and representatives from each reservation, is the chief governing body of the Seminole Tribe of Florida.
Adding the Tampa and Immokalee reservations brought the Seminole Tribe of Florida's federal trust lands to more than 90,000 acres.

nations.name: Southeastern Mvskoke Nation
nations.lands: Near Troy in Alabama; its history describes organization around Pike and Coffee Counties.

facts.text: The Nation presents its language page as a small learning resource for Tribal members and other Mvskokes.
Its introduction locates the Nation near Troy in Alabama.

nations.name: Delaware Tribe of Indians
nations.lands: Bartlesville, Oklahoma, United States; homelands along the Delaware River

facts.text: The Delaware Tribe of Indians is a federally recognized tribe of the Lenape people, headquartered in Bartlesville, Oklahoma.
The Tribe's online Lenape Talking Dictionary holds about 15,380 words, along with recorded stories and songs, and is still growing.

source.title: Language Revitalization - Delaware Tribe of Indians

pronounce.publisher: Delaware Tribe of Indians, on its own site

nations.name: Sappony
nations.lands: the High Plains Indian Settlement along the North Carolina-Virginia boundary, including Person County, North Carolina, and Halifax County, Virginia, as described by Sappony

facts.text: Sappony describes committees addressing education, cultural preservation and economic development.
Sappony's governance page describes a council with one elected representative from each of the settlement's seven families.

nations.name: The Chickasaw Nation
nations.lands: Thirteen counties in south-central Oklahoma, United States; original homelands in present-day Mississippi, Alabama and Tennessee

facts.text: The Chickasaw Nation's three-department government was reestablished with the ratification of its 1983 Constitution.
The Chickasaw language revitalization program began in 2007, and its master-apprentice program pairs learners with fluent Chickasaw speakers.

nations.name: Catawba Nation
nations.lands: York County, South Carolina, near Rock Hill, with a service area that includes North Carolina, United States

facts.text: After a 20-year effort, a land claim settlement on November 20, 1993 brought the Catawba Indian Nation federal recognition.
The Catawba Nation has over 3,300 enrolled citizens and continues to grow.

nations.name: Haliwa-Saponi Indian Tribe
nations.lands: the Meadows area at present-day Hollister, North Carolina; the Tribe locates its government there without defining territorial boundaries in this source

facts.text: The Tribe describes Red Earth as a program for all ages to learn about Haliwa-Saponi history and cultural practices.

source.title: Cultural Classes - Haliwa Saponi Tribe Resources

facts.text: The Tribal School's stated mission combines academics, technology and community involvement with American Indian culture.

source.title: Haliwa Saponi Tribal School: Quality Education - Haliwa Saponi Tribe Resources

nations.name: Waccamaw Siouan Tribe
nations.lands: Bladen and Columbus Counties in southeastern North Carolina, near Green Swamp

facts.text: Its government page describes a Tribal Council elected by the membership and an Elders Review Committee.
The Tribe's introduction places its communities mainly in Bladen and Columbus Counties, North Carolina, near Green Swamp.

nations.name: Onondaga Nation
nations.lands: Onondaga Nation territory south of Syracuse, central New York, United States

facts.text: In the Haudenosaunee Grand Council, the Onondaga Fire Keepers present an issue, and debate goes on until they can announce that all are of One Mind, a decision by consensus.
The Onondaga Nation is still governed by its traditional government, with fourteen Chiefs and their Clan Mothers serving as caretakers of the land.

nations.name: Shinnecock Indian Nation
nations.lands: In and around the Town of Southampton on the eastern end of Long Island, New York, United States

facts.text: On October 1, 2010, the Shinnecock Indian Nation was formally recognized by the United States as the 565th federally recognized tribe.
The Shinnecock Indian Nation has over 1,589 enrolled tribal members.

nations.name: Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia
nations.lands: southeastern Virginia along the Nottoway River; the Tribe's Community House & Interpretive Center is in Capron

facts.text: The Tribe's history describes the Nottoway as Iroquoian speakers of southeastern Virginia.

source.title: Tribal History - Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia

facts.text: The Tribe says its Community House & Interpretive Center formally opened in Capron on May 5, 2012.

source.title: Community House & Interpretive Center - Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia

nations.name: Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina
nations.lands: Along the Lumbee River in Robeson, Hoke, Cumberland and Scotland counties, North Carolina, United States, centered on Pembroke

facts.text: The Lumbee Tribe became fully federally recognized by the United States on December 18, 2025.
The Lumbee Tribe describes its people, the People of the Dark Water, as entrepreneurial and strongly focused on education.

nations.name: Oneida Indian Nation
nations.lands: Central New York, United States

facts.text: Oneida Indian Nation Members learn Onyota’a:ká:, the Oneida language, through intensive courses, a preschool curriculum, e-books, smartphone apps and an Oneida language keyboard.
During the American Revolution, Oneidas fought alongside the colonists and carried corn to feed General Washington's starving soldiers; the Nation honors them as America's first allies.

nations.name: Osage Nation
nations.lands: Osage Nation Reservation, northeastern Oklahoma, United States; headquarters in Pawhuska

facts.text: The Osage Minerals Council, an elected body of eight members, is part of the Osage Nation's government.
Since 2006 the Osage Nation has governed itself under a constitution with separate executive, legislative and judicial branches.

nations.name: Standing Rock Sioux Tribe
nations.lands: Standing Rock Reservation, across North Dakota and South Dakota, United States

facts.text: Today Yanktonai Dakota communities live mostly on the North Dakota side of Standing Rock, and Lakota communities mostly on the South Dakota side.
The Standing Rock Tribal Council has a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, Secretary and 14 council members, all elected by tribal members for four-year terms.

source.title: Standing Rock Sioux Tribe | Indian Affairs Commission, North Dakota

nations.name: Pawnee Nation of Oklahoma
nations.lands: Pawnee, Oklahoma, United States; ancestral homeland on the central Plains

facts.text: The Pawnee Business Council is the supreme governing body of the Pawnee Nation, acting within the nation's Constitution and federal law.
The Pawnee Nation is made up of four bands: the Čawî’ (Grand), Kitkahaki (Republican), Pitahawirata (Tappage) and Skidi (Wolf).

source.title: Pawnee History | Pawnee Nation of Oklahoma

nations.name: Ponca Tribe of Nebraska
nations.lands: Fifteen-county service area across Nebraska, Iowa and South Dakota, United States

facts.text: The tribe serves its people across a fifteen-county service area in Nebraska, Iowa and South Dakota, set up by the Ponca Restoration Act.
The Ponca Restoration Act, signed by President George H. W. Bush, restored federal recognition to the Ponca Tribe of Nebraska.

nations.name: Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe
nations.lands: Cheyenne River Reservation, central South Dakota, United States; headquarters in Eagle Butte

facts.text: The tribe is governed by a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, Secretary, Treasurer and fifteen council members, with headquarters in Eagle Butte.

source.title: Cheyenne River Agency | Indian Affairs
source.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs

facts.text: The Cheyenne River Reservation holds about 1.45 million trust acres in Ziebach and Dewey counties in central South Dakota.

source.title: Cheyenne River Agency | Indian Affairs
source.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs

nations.name: Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska
nations.lands: Reservation along the Kansas and Nebraska border, United States

facts.text: The tribe is governed by two bodies, a General Council and an Executive Committee.

source.title: Welcome to the Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska
source.publisher: Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska

facts.text: The reservation of the Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska straddles the eastern border between the two states, and tribal headquarters is on it.

source.title: Welcome to the Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska
source.publisher: Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska

nations.name: Citizen Potawatomi Nation
nations.lands: Headquartered in Shawnee, Oklahoma, United States, with citizens around the world

facts.text: In July 2026 the Citizen Potawatomi Nation signed the articles of confederation for the Potawatomi Confederacy.
The Citizen Potawatomi Nation Constitution dates from 1938 and was amended in 1985 and again in 2007.

nations.name: Kaw Nation
nations.lands: Oklahoma, with historical homelands in Kansas and the Great Plains

facts.text: The Nation's history distinguishes a Tribal Council from a General Council composed of enrolled adult citizens.
The Nation's language page lists online learning and a basic Kanza course. Listed materials remain under the publisher's access and use conditions.

nations.name: Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate
nations.lands: Lake Traverse Reservation, northeastern South Dakota and southeastern North Dakota, United States

facts.text: The Lake Traverse Reservation reaches across seven counties, five in South Dakota and two in North Dakota.
The Oyate counts more than 14,000 tribal members, living across the United States and serving abroad in the Armed Forces.

nations.name: Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes
nations.lands: Western Oklahoma, United States; headquarters in Concho

facts.text: The Cheyenne and Arapaho Language Program offers classes in tribal communities and online for tribal members.

source.title: Language and Culture | Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes

facts.text: The tribes run adult immersion training aimed at producing functionally fluent speakers of both the Cheyenne and Arapaho languages.

source.title: Language and Culture | Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes

nations.name: Meskwaki Nation
also: Sac & Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa
nations.lands: Meskwaki Settlement near Tama, Iowa, United States

facts.text: The Meskwaki Nation has its own constitution, codified laws, police officers and a fully functioning court system.

source.title: History | Meskwaki | Sac & Fox Tribe of the Mississippi
source.publisher: Sac & Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa

facts.text: The Meskwaki language is close to the Sauk and Kickapoo dialects, and the people are working hard to keep it strong.

source.title: History | Meskwaki | Sac & Fox Tribe of the Mississippi
source.publisher: Sac & Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa

nations.name: Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community
nations.lands: Scott County, Minnesota, United States

facts.text: Following the Dakota tradition of helping others, the SMSC gives millions of dollars each year to other tribes, organizations and local governments.

source.title: Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community in Scott County, MN

facts.text: The community says plainly that it is still here, living traditional Dakota lifeways that will pass on to future generations.

source.title: Our History - Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community in Scott County, MN

nations.name: Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians
nations.lands: Northern Lower Peninsula of Michigan, United States

facts.text: The tribe is governed by a nine-member Tribal Council whose members serve staggered terms.

source.title: Home - LTBB Official Website
source.publisher: Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians

facts.text: The tribe's mission celebrates that its people still have and speak their own language, Anishinaabemowin.

source.title: Home - LTBB Official Website
source.publisher: Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians

nations.name: Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin
nations.lands: Menominee Reservation, northeastern Wisconsin, United States

facts.text: The Menominee Tribal Legislature has nine members.
The Menominee Reservation covers about 235,524 acres in Wisconsin and holds the largest single tract of virgin timberland in the state.

nations.name: Otoe-Missouria Tribe
nations.lands: Red Rock, Oklahoma; historical homelands include Nebraska and the lower Missouri River valley

facts.text: The Tribe's government page describes a seven-member Tribal Council elected by qualified Tribal voters using a secret ballot.
The Tribe's preservation page dates National Park Service recognition of its Tribal Historic Preservation Office to spring 2016.

nations.name: Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes
nations.lands: Fort Peck Reservation, northeastern Montana, United States; headquarters in Poplar

facts.text: Members of the Fort Peck Tribal Executive Board, except the secretary-accountant, are elected at-large every two years.

source.title: Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes
source.publisher: Montana Governor's Office of Indian Affairs

facts.text: The Fort Peck Reservation in northeastern Montana includes more than two million acres of land.

source.title: Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes
source.publisher: Montana Governor's Office of Indian Affairs

nations.name: Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation
nations.lands: Reservation near Mayetta, northeastern Kansas, United States

facts.text: The Nation has offered Potawatomi language classes since 2007 as part of its work to revitalize the language and culture.

source.title: Prairie Band Potawatomi Language Revitalization Efforts

facts.text: The Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation says its Kansas reservation is unchanged from what the Treaty of 1846 established.

source.title: Prairie Band Potawatomi Tribal History: Origins, Separation, and Stewardship

nations.name: Ho-Chunk Nation
nations.lands: Wisconsin, United States, on lands in many places rather than one reservation; traditional lands also reach Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri and Illinois

facts.text: The Ho-Chunk Nation has four branches of government, with a legislature of 13 members elected from four districts.
Alongside its constitutional government, the Ho-Chunk Nation keeps a traditional system of leadership based on chiefs and clans.

nations.name: Sicangu Lakota Oyate
nations.lands: Rosebud Reservation, South Dakota, United States

facts.text: The tribe's history page says the Lakota number about 70,000 today, and that about a third of them still speak their ancestral language.
The Rosebud Reservation takes in 20 communities, and the tribal headquarters is in the community of Rosebud, South Dakota.

nations.name: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation
nations.lands: Treaty 6 territory in central Saskatchewan, Canada, with urban reserve land in Saskatoon

facts.text: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation planned a gathering for August 20 to 23, 2026 to mark 150 years since Treaty 6 was signed.

source.title: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation, Band No. 102

facts.text: In 1988 Muskeg Lake Cree Nation created Asimakeniseekan Askiy in Saskatoon, the first commercial urban reserve in Canada.

nations.name: Gitxsan
nations.lands: The Laxyip along the upper Skeena River and its tributaries in northern British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: Gitxsan society is matriarchal, with four clans made up of independent Houses (Huwilp), each led by a Wii Simoogit, or high chief.
Gitxsanimaax, the traditional Gitxsan language, has two dialects: Giigeenix, spoken up river, and Gyeets, spoken down river.

nations.name: Piikani Nation
nations.lands: Around Brocket in southern Alberta, Canada, near the Old Man River; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

facts.text: Piikani stories, ceremonies and songs describe an ancestral territory reaching north to the North Saskatchewan River and west into the Rocky Mountains.
Piikani Nation had 3,928 registered members as of September 2026.

source.title: First Nation Profiles: Registered Population (Piikani Nation)
source.publisher: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada

nations.name: Atikamekw
nations.lands: Nitaskinan in central Quebec, Canada, with the communities of Manawan, Wemotaci and Opitciwan

facts.text: The Atikamekw language, like other Algonquin and Anishinaabe languages, is rich in imagery and names things by how they truly are.
Young people aged 0 to 35 make up about 65 percent of the Atikamekw population today.

nations.name: Innu
nations.lands: Nitassinan: Labrador (Newfoundland and Labrador) and eastern Quebec, Canada

facts.text: In 2008 the Innu Nation and Newfoundland and Labrador signed the Tshash Petapen, or New Dawn, Agreement.

source.title: Innu Nation of Labrador
source.publisher: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Indigenous Affairs and Reconciliation

facts.text: The Innu Nation land claim, accepted for negotiation in 1978, covers about 70 percent of Labrador.

source.title: Innu Nation of Labrador
source.publisher: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Indigenous Affairs and Reconciliation

nations.name: Six Nations of the Grand River
nations.lands: Along the Grand River in southern Ontario, Canada

facts.text: It is the only First Nation community home to all six Haudenosaunee nations: Mohawk, Cayuga, Onondaga, Oneida, Seneca and Tuscarora.

source.title: Who We Are
source.publisher: Six Nations of the Grand River

facts.text: No First Nation in Canada has a larger population than Six Nations of the Grand River.

source.title: Who We Are
source.publisher: Six Nations of the Grand River

nations.name: Haíɫzaqv
nations.lands: The Central Coast of British Columbia, Canada, centred on Bella Bella (Wáglísla) on Campbell Island

facts.text: In 2025 Heiltsuk members ratified a written constitution, a milestone in self-governance.
Haíɫzaqv means 'to speak and act correctly', principles that guide Heiltsuk ancestral and present-day ways of life.

nations.name: Tłı̨chǫ
nations.lands: Between Great Slave Lake and Great Bear Lake in the Northwest Territories, Canada, around the communities of Behchokǫ̀, Whatì, Gamètì and Wekweètì

facts.text: The Tłı̨chǫ Agreement, in effect since August 4, 2005, was the first combined land, resources and self-government agreement in the Northwest Territories.

source.title: Concluding and Implementing Land and Resources and Self-Government Agreements: Tłı̨chǫ
source.publisher: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs

facts.text: The Tłı̨chǫ Government makes laws for its citizens in areas including education, child and family services, and Tłı̨chǫ language and culture.

source.title: Concluding and Implementing Land and Resources and Self-Government Agreements: Tłı̨chǫ
source.publisher: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs

nations.name: Secwépemc
nations.lands: Secwepemcúl’ecw, a large territory in the interior of British Columbia, Canada, stretching from the Columbia River valley west to the Fraser River

facts.text: The Shuswap Nation Tribal Council brings together nine Secwépemc communities in the Southern Interior of British Columbia.
Secwépemc Chiefs formed the Shuswap Nation Tribal Council in 1980 to advance Aboriginal rights, self-government and the settlement of land title.

nations.name: Anishinabek Nation
nations.lands: 39 First Nations across Ontario, Canada, from Pikwàkanagàn in the east and Aamjiwnaang in the south to Lake Nipigon in the north

facts.text: It is Ontario's oldest political organization, with roots in the Confederacy of Three Fires that long predates European contact.
The Anishinabek Nation speaks for 39 First Nations in Ontario with about 70,000 citizens, roughly one third of the province's First Nation population.

nations.name: Dene
nations.lands: Denendeh, the western Northwest Territories, Canada

facts.text: The Dene Nation brings together five regional groups, the Gwich'in, Sahtú, Deh Cho, Tłı̨chǫ and Akaitcho Dene, each with its own language and territory.
Dene simply means 'the people'. Their homeland, Denendeh, lies in the western Northwest Territories.

nations.name: Labrador Inuit
nations.lands: Nunatsiavut, on the north coast of Labrador, Canada

facts.text: Nunatsiavut's legislative capital is Hopedale and its administrative capital is Nain.
The Nunatsiavut Government, the self-government of Labrador Inuit, officially came into being on December 1, 2005.

nations.name: Nisg̱a’a Nation
nations.lands: The Nass River Valley (K’alii-Aksim-Lisims) in northwestern British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Nisg̱a’a, People of the Nass River, are a self-governing First Nation on Canada's Pacific Coast.
The Nisg̱a’a Final Agreement was the first modern treaty in British Columbia, and it recognizes both Nisg̱a’a Lands and the Nisg̱a’a Government.

nations.name: Métis Nation
nations.lands: The Métis Nation Homeland as described by the Métis National Council: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, plus parts of Ontario, British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and the northern United States

facts.text: Many historic Métis communities still stand along rivers and lakes once tied to fur trade posts, and many Métis citizens live in cities within the Homeland.
The Métis emerged as a distinct Indigenous people with their own culture, traditions, nationhood and language, Michif.

nations.name: Ktunaxa
nations.lands: ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa: the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia, Canada, with Kootenay Tribes also based today in Montana and Idaho, United States

facts.text: The Ktunaxa Nation Council helps represent the shared interests of four Ktunaxa First Nations within ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the Ktunaxa homelands.
ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the traditional territory, covers about 70,000 square kilometres in the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia.

nations.name: Mi’kmaq
nations.lands: Mi’kma’ki: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and the Gaspé in Canada, with relatives in Maine, United States

facts.text: Mi'kmaw communities in Nova Scotia wrote their own Netukulimk Livelihood Management Plans so members who fish can support themselves and their families.
In 2006 the 13 Mi'kmaw Chiefs of Nova Scotia formed the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs to guide the Nation's negotiators on rights and title.

nations.name: Tsuut’ina Nation
nations.lands: Treaty 7 territory in southern Alberta, Canada, bordering the city of Calgary

facts.text: Tsuut'ina Nation describes itself today as a highly sufficient and economically advanced First Nation.
Tsuut'ina is the only Dene-speaking nation in Treaty 7 territory, linked to the wider Dene Nation by its Athabaskan language.

nations.name: Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation
nations.lands: Old Crow and the surrounding homeland in northern Yukon, Canada

facts.text: Old Crow, a fly-in community of about 300 people on the Porcupine River, is the seat of the Vuntut Gwitchin government.
Dinjii Zhuh k'yuu, the Gwich'in language, is the official language of the Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation, which is training teachers and raising young speakers.

nations.name: Southern Ute Indian Tribe
nations.lands: Southern Ute Reservation around Ignacio, southwestern Colorado, United States

facts.text: The Southern Ute Indian Tribe is made up of the Mouache and Caputa bands and is headquartered in Ignacio, Colorado.
An elected Tribal Council governs the Southern Ute Indian Tribe, which maintains its own constitution, laws and tribal courts.

nations.name: San Carlos Apache
nations.lands: Gila, Graham and Pinal counties, southeastern Arizona, US

facts.text: The San Carlos Apache Reservation, set aside in 1871, covers 1,834,781 acres reaching from alpine meadows to desert in southeastern Arizona.
More than a third of San Carlos land is forest or woodland, giving a home to elk, mule deer, black bear, turkeys and mountain lion.

nations.name: A:shiwi
nations.lands: Pueblo of Zuni along the Zuni River in western New Mexico, US, with reservation land in Arizona

facts.text: The Pueblo of Zuni counts about 18,692 people and holds about 463,287 acres of reservation land.
For about the last 300 years most Zuni people have lived in one main village, the Pueblo of Zuni, with farming villages used at planting and harvest.

nations.name: Lipan Apache Tribe
nations.lands: Texas, United States, with tribal administration in McAllen and historical homelands spanning Texas and northern Mexico

facts.text: The Lipan Apache Tribe in Texas maintains a Tribal Council responsible for community welfare and protection of its heritage.
In 2021, the City and County of Presidio donated a Lipan cemetery parcel to the Lipan Apache Tribe.

source.title: El Cementerio de los Lipanes Transferred to Tribe

nations.name: Ute Indian Tribe
also: Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
nations.lands: Uintah and Ouray Reservation, northeastern Utah, with tribal government at Fort Duchesne, United States

facts.text: In an April 2026 statement, the Ute Indian Tribe announced it would appeal a federal district court decision concerning split-estate reservation lands.

source.title: Tribe will appeal Utah Federal District Court decision on split estate lands

facts.text: The Ute Indian Tribe elects Business Committee representatives from the Uintah, Uncompahgre and Whiteriver bands.

nations.name: Taos Pueblo
nations.lands: Taos valley, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: Tiwa is the native language of Taos Pueblo, and English and Spanish are also spoken there.
In 1970 a federal law returned 48,000 acres, including Blue Lake, to Taos Pueblo, a landmark for tribal self-determination across the United States.

nations.name: Wixárika
nations.lands: Sierra Madre Occidental in Jalisco and Nayarit, Mexico, with communities in Durango and Zacatecas

facts.text: At the end of the 1700s Wixárika communities received land titles that defined the boundaries of their present-day communities.

source.title: Huicholes
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: In July 2025 UNESCO added the Wixárika Route through sacred sites to Wirikuta, a 500 km corridor, to the World Heritage List after decades of Wixaritari requests.

source.title: Boletín No. 334: La Ruta Wixárika por los sitios sagrados a Wirikuta es inscrita en la Lista de Patrimonio Mundial de la UNESCO
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH)

nations.name: Acoma
nations.lands: Acoma Mesa and surrounding lands in west-central New Mexico, US

facts.text: Since 2017 the Acoma Language Program has been building a Keres dictionary, with about 5,000 words and phrases being edited by fluent speakers.
In 1999 Acoma set up a Historic Preservation Office to keep traditional skills alive, among them stone cutting, wood carving, pottery making and weaving.

nations.name: Southern Paiute
nations.lands: Southern Utah and northern Arizona, US, including Cedar City, Utah, and the Kaibab reservation near Fredonia, Arizona

facts.text: The Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah Restoration Act of April 3, 1980 brought formal federal recognition to the Cedar Band of Paiute Indians.
The Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah shares The Paiute Language for Beginners, now in its second edition, which anyone can view and download.

nations.name: Rarámuri
nations.lands: Sierra Tarahumara in Chihuahua, Mexico, with smaller communities in Durango, Sonora and Sinaloa

facts.text: Rarámuri artisans make violins, drums, palm baskets, clay pots and wooden masks, and sell them in towns such as Guachochi, Creel and Batopilas.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: The Rarámuri ball race is a contest in which runners cover long distances while kicking a wooden ball, and it is held as part of community fiestas.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Tohono O’odham
nations.lands: Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona, US (Sells is the capital), with O’odham communities across the border in Sonora, Mexico

facts.text: Divided by the border since the 1850s, O’odham communities in Sonora, Mexico, and Arizona still share a common culture and sense of being one people.

source.title: Pápagos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: O’odham groups still speak the O’odham language, part of the Uto-Aztecan family, with dialects that vary from group to group.

nations.name: Hopi
nations.lands: Hopitutskwa, northeastern Arizona, US (Navajo and Coconino counties)

facts.text: Hopi government is unicameral. Its powers rest with a Tribal Council of village representatives, who serve two year terms.
The Hopi Reservation in northeastern Arizona covers more than 1.5 million acres and is made up of 12 villages on three mesas.

source.title: The Official Website of the Hopi Tribe

nations.name: Kha’P’o
nations.lands: From the eastern Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: People of Santa Clara Pueblo still speak the Tewa language today and carry on their customs and cultural activities.
Santa Clara is one of six Tewa-speaking villages, and its reservation covers about 90 square miles from the Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande.

nations.name: Kumeyaay
nations.lands: San Diego and Imperial counties, California, US, and Tecate, Ensenada and Rosarito in Baja California, Mexico

facts.text: North of the US and Mexico border there are 12 Kumeyaay Nation bands today, each original to Kumeyaay territory. Sycuan is one of them.

source.title: History & Heritage
source.publisher: Sycuan Band of the Kumeyaay Nation

facts.text: In Baja California the Kumiai call themselves Tipai. Their communities sit on the coastal plateaus of Ensenada and Rosarito and in Tecate.

source.title: Kumiais
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Yoeme
nations.lands: Yaqui River valley in Sonora, Mexico, and Pascua Yaqui communities near Tucson, Arizona, US

facts.text: Most Yoeme people today live in the Mexican states of Sonora and Sinaloa, and the federally recognized Pascua Yaqui Tribe is based in Tucson, Arizona.
The Pascua Yaqui Tribe in Arizona gained United States federal recognition on September 18, 1978.

nations.name: Chiricahua Apache Nation
nations.lands: Headquarters in Santa Clara, New Mexico, United States; this record describes this named community, not every Chiricahua Apache person or government

facts.text: The Chiricahua Apache Nation lists its tribal headquarters in Santa Clara, New Mexico.
Its foundation's stated work includes education, social welfare and defending Chiricahua Apache self-determination.

nations.name: Shipibo-Konibo
nations.lands: Ucayali, Madre de Dios, Loreto and Huánuco in Peru, with an urban community at Cantagallo in Lima

facts.text: Cantagallo, home to Shipibo-Konibo families, is the best known Amazonian Indigenous settlement in metropolitan Lima.

source.title: Shipibo-Konibo | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Peru's 2017 national census, 25,232 people identified as part of the Shipibo-Konibo people.

source.title: Shipibo-Konibo | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Tupinambá
nations.lands: Atlantic Forest of southern Bahia around Olivença, in Ilhéus, Buerarema and Una, with Tupinambá communities also in Pará, Brazil

facts.text: The Tupinambá of Olivença live in the Atlantic Forest region of southern Bahia.
In 2001 Funai, Brazil's Indigenous affairs agency, officially recognized the Tupinambá of Olivença as an Indigenous people.

nations.name: Guarani Kaiowá
nations.lands: Southern Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, and neighboring eastern Paraguay, where the people are known as Paĩ Tavyterã

facts.text: Kaiowá, Ñandeva and Mbya Guarani all speak dialects of Guarani and show strong energy in keeping their language alive.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

facts.text: Guarani communities today call the places they live tekoha, a word that joins land, forest, fields, water, animals, plants and medicines.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

nations.name: Mẽbêngôkre
nations.lands: Forests and savannas of southern Pará and northern Mato Grosso, Brazil, along rivers of the Xingu basin such as the Iriri, Bacajá and Fresco

facts.text: The Associação Floresta Protegida, created in 1998 by Mẽbêngôkre leaders, represents about 3,000 people in 31 villages across three Indigenous lands.
The Mẽbêngôkre language belongs to the Jê family of the Macro-Jê language stock.

nations.name: Yanomami
nations.lands: Forests of Amazonas and Roraima states in northern Brazil, continuing across the border into southern Venezuela

facts.text: The Yanomami language family is not linked to any other language stock, and it has six languages and sixteen dialects.

source.title: TI Yanomami
source.publisher: Casa Civil da Presidência da República, Governo do Brasil

facts.text: The Yanomami Indigenous Territory in Brazil, about 9.66 million hectares of tropical forest, was ratified by presidential decree on 25 May 1992.

nations.name: Awajún
nations.lands: Northern Peruvian Amazon in Amazonas, Loreto, San Martín, Cajamarca and Ucayali

facts.text: The Federation of Aguaruna Women of the Upper Marañón (FEMAAM), founded in Imaza in 2002, opened the way for Awajún women's political participation.

source.title: Awajún | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: The Awajún language belongs to the Jivaroan language family.

source.title: Awajún | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Wichí
nations.lands: Gran Chaco of northern Argentina, mainly Salta, Formosa and Chaco provinces, with related communities in southern Bolivia

facts.text: In 2010 Argentina's Chaco province made the Wichí, Qom and Moqoit languages official languages of the province alongside Spanish.

source.title: Argentine: les lois provinciales à portée linguistique
source.publisher: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde, Université Laval (CEFAN)

nations.name: Pueblo Originario Kichwa de Sarayaku
nations.lands: Middle Bobonaza river basin, Pastaza province, Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: About 1,500 Kichwa people of Sarayaku live in seven community centers across roughly 135,000 hectares on the Bobonaza river in Pastaza, Ecuador.
Sarayaku has its own statute on image, communication and digital sovereignty, setting free, prior and informed consent rules for visitors, press and researchers.

source.title: Statute of Governance of Image, Communication, and Digital Sovereignty of the Kichwa Indigenous People of Sarayaku

nations.name: Qom
nations.lands: Gran Chaco of northern Argentina, especially Chaco, Formosa and Santa Fe provinces, plus communities in Buenos Aires and in Paraguay

facts.text: The Qom language is being recovered in universities and in community-run spaces, and children and teenagers are taking it up.

source.title: El wichí y el qom comienzan a ser hablados en la primera infancia y en la adolescencia
source.publisher: Unidiversidad, Universidad Nacional de Cuyo (from Télam)

facts.text: Qom is one of three Indigenous languages that Argentina's Chaco province declared official alongside Spanish in 2010.

source.title: Argentine: les lois provinciales à portée linguistique
source.publisher: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde, Université Laval (CEFAN)

nations.name: Munduruku
nations.lands: Tapajós river basin in Pará, with communities in Amazonas and Mato Grosso, Brazil

facts.text: Munduruku of the upper Tapajós created the Pusuru Indigenous Association in 1991 as a formal way to organize their communities.
The Munduruku language belongs to its own Munduruku family within the Tupi language stock.

nations.name: Waorani
nations.lands: Orellana, Pastaza and Napo provinces in the Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: Waorani territory includes 32 communities in three Amazonian provinces of Ecuador: Orellana, Pastaza and Napo.
The legally recognized Waorani territory is governed by NAWE, the Waorani Nationality of Ecuador, regarded as the highest Waorani territorial authority.

nations.name: Huni Kuin
nations.lands: Rivers of Acre state in western Brazil, such as the Tarauacá, Jordão and Purus, and the Purus and Curanja rivers in Peru

facts.text: Huni kuin, the name the people use for themselves, means true people, or people with known customs.

source.title: Huni Kuin (Kaxinawá) - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

facts.text: MAHKU, the Huni Kuin Artists Movement founded in Acre in 2013, painted a large mural across the facade of the Central Pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale.

source.title: Biennale Arte 2024 | MAHKU (Movimento dos Artistas Huni Kuin)

nations.name: Tsimane'
nations.lands: Forests and savannas of the Beni department, Bolivia, mainly along the Maniquí and Apere rivers

facts.text: Tsimane' livelihoods center on small farms of plantains, rice, corn and sweet manioc, along with fishing, hunting and gathering.

source.title: Tsimane fieldsite in Bolivia
source.publisher: Culture and the Mind project, University of Sheffield

facts.text: Almost all Tsimane' speak their own Tsimane' language as their main language.

source.title: Tsimane fieldsite in Bolivia
source.publisher: Culture and the Mind project, University of Sheffield

nations.name: Asháninka
nations.lands: Central Peruvian Amazon in Junín, Ucayali, Pasco, Cusco, Huánuco and Ayacucho

facts.text: In 2017, 73,567 people in Peru said Ashaninka was the language they learned to speak as children.

source.title: Ashaninka | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Peru's 2017 national census, 55,493 people identified as part of the Asháninka people.

source.title: Ashaninka | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Puyallup Tribe of Indians
nations.lands: Shores of southern Puget Sound and the Puyallup River, Tacoma area, Washington

facts.text: One of the most urban tribes in the United States, the Puyallup still fish, hunt and travel the waters of the Puyallup River.
The Tribe gives its name as puyaləpabš, meaning people at the bend at the bottom of the river.

nations.name: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe
nations.lands: Death Valley and surrounding areas of California and Nevada

facts.text: Today the federally recognized Timbisha Shoshone Tribe works to keep its language, traditions and sovereignty strong.

source.title: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe - California and Nevada

facts.text: The Timbisha, part of the larger Western Shoshone people, have lived in Death Valley and its surrounding areas for thousands of years, and their village sits inside Death Valley National Park.

source.title: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe - California and Nevada

nations.name: Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria
nations.lands: Sonoma and Marin counties, California, with a reservation near Rohnert Park

facts.text: Graton Rancheria launched its own Tribal TANF program serving low-income Native American families in Sonoma and Marin counties.
Graton Rancheria, a federation of Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo groups, regained federal recognition through a law signed on December 27, 2000.

nations.name: Yurok Tribe
nations.lands: Lower Klamath River and the Pacific coast of far northern California, United States

facts.text: When Yurok people speak of themselves, they say Oohl, which means Indian people.
On June 30, 2026, Save the Redwoods League conveyed 125 acres on Prairie Creek, in the heart of Yurok ancestral territory, back to the Yurok Tribe.

nations.name: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation
nations.lands: South-central Washington State, around Mount Adams and tributaries of the Columbia River

facts.text: The Yakama Nation shares an Ichishkiin word each day to help learners build fluency in the language, also called Sahaptin.

source.title: Ichishkiin Word of the Day: Learn New Vocabulary | Yakama Nation
source.publisher: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation

facts.text: The Yakama Reservation in Washington State spans about 1,130,000 acres.

source.title: About
source.publisher: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation

nations.name: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians
nations.lands: Santa Ynez Valley, Santa Barbara County, California

facts.text: The Tribe's Culture Department founded its language program in 2008, and the Tribe has unveiled a Samala-English Dictionary.

source.title: Culture
source.publisher: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians

facts.text: Established on December 27, 1901, the Santa Ynez Reservation began with 99 acres and has grown to more than 1,500 acres.

source.title: The Santa Ynez Reservation
source.publisher: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians

nations.name: Tongva
nations.lands: Greater Los Angeles region of California, a homeland called Tovaangar

facts.text: The conservancy, a Tongva-led nonprofit and not a tribal government, serves Tongva people, the wider Native community and guests, called kuuyam.
In 2022 Huhuunga, a one-acre parcel in Altadena, was returned to Tongva stewardship. It is now home to the Tongva-led Tongva Taraxat Paxaavxa Conservancy.

nations.name: Muckleshoot Indian Tribe
nations.lands: South King County, Washington, in the Puget Sound region; ancestors include Duwamish and Upper Puyallup peoples

facts.text: The Muckleshoot Indian Tribe is one of South King County's largest employers, supporting about 3,300 direct jobs.
Among Puget Sound tribes, Muckleshoot is the only one holding rights under two treaties.

nations.name: Tulalip Tribes
nations.lands: Tulalip Indian Reservation on Puget Sound, Snohomish County, Washington

facts.text: The Tulalip Lushootseed Language Department works toward every tribal home, workplace, gathering and classroom being rich in Lushootseed.
The Tulalip Tribes count over 5,100 people, about 2,700 of whom live on the 22,000-acre Tulalip Indian Reservation.

pronounce.publisher: Tulalip Tribes, on its own site

nations.name: Kashia Band of Pomo Indians
also: Kashia Band of Pomo Indians of the Stewarts Point Rancheria
nations.lands: Sonoma County coast of California, from the Gualala River south toward the Russian River

facts.text: The Kashia Band owns the 688-acre Kashia Coastal Reserve, which spans both sides of Highway 1 just north of Salt Point State Park.
Kashia homelands reached from the Gualala River in the north to Duncan's Point, south of the Russian River.

nations.name: Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs
nations.lands: Central Oregon, stretching east from the summit of the Cascade Mountains

facts.text: The Museum at Warm Springs shares the history and culture of the three tribes and welcomes visitors in Ichishkiin, Numu and Kiksht.

source.title: Museum at Warm Springs - Culture. History. In Living Color.

facts.text: In 1937 the Warm Springs, Wasco and Paiute organized as one confederated government under their own constitution and bylaws.

nations.name: Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation
nations.lands: Smith River and the coast of Del Norte County, far northern California

facts.text: The Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation was restored in 1983 through a court case, and its restored government extended citizenship to all Taa-laa-wa Dee-ni'.
Tolowa Dee-ni' language work goes back to a language program formed in 1969, and the Nation calls revitalization vital to Tolowa identity.

nations.name: Makah Tribe
nations.lands: Neah Bay and Cape Flattery, at the northwest tip of Washington's Olympic Peninsula

facts.text: The name Makah came from neighboring tribes and means people generous with food.
The Makah Reservation at Neah Bay sits on the northwest tip of the continental United States.

nations.name: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation
nations.lands: Umatilla Indian Reservation in northeastern Oregon, home of the Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla peoples

facts.text: CTUIR teaches the Umatilla, Walla Walla and Weyíiletpuu (Cayuse) languages to all ages, drawing on the knowledge of fluent speakers.

source.title: Languages of the CTUIR
source.publisher: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation

facts.text: Nixyáawii, the homeland name used by the Tribes' language program, means the place of many springs.

source.title: Languages of the CTUIR
source.publisher: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation

nations.name: Te-Moak Tribe of Western Shoshone Indians
nations.lands: Northeastern Nevada, in Battle Mountain, Elko, South Fork and Wells

facts.text: The Te-Moak Tribe unites four bands, Battle Mountain, Elko, South Fork and Wells, under one tribal council elected every three years.
Western Shoshone people are descendants of an ancient, widespread people whose name, Newe, means The People.

nations.name: Mam
nations.lands: Western highlands of Guatemala (Huehuetenango, San Marcos, Quetzaltenango) and neighboring Chiapas, Mexico

facts.text: In October 2025, the Mam communities of Cajolá and Todos Santos Cuchumatán joined two other Maya communities in reporting to a UN committee on their community radio rights.

source.title: Indigenous Communities and Cultural Survival Urge CERD to Address Community Radio Rights Violations in Guatemala

facts.text: B'alam Stereo in Cabricán, among the longer-running Indigenous stations in Guatemala's highlands, has served the Maya Mam since 1976, with work promoting education, health, water and justice.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

nations.name: Lokono
nations.lands: Coastal and river villages of Suriname, Guyana and French Guiana

facts.text: Suriname's association of Indigenous village leaders lists the Lokono among the country's four major Indigenous peoples, with villages such as Washabo, Apoera and Alfonsdorp.

source.title: Dorpen en Dorpsbesturen
source.publisher: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)

facts.text: Lokono village representatives founded Wadian Bokotothi, meaning 'Language Keepers', and helped share one common Lokono spelling across Suriname, French Guiana and Guyana.

source.title: State-of-the-Art in the Development of the Lokono Language
source.publisher: Language Documentation & Conservation, University of Hawai'i Press

nations.name: Ch'orti'
nations.lands: Jocotán, Camotán, Olopa and Quezaltepeque in Chiquimula and La Unión in Zacapa, Guatemala, and communities around Copán in Honduras

facts.text: Ch'orti' is also spoken in Honduran communities such as Cabañas, Santa Rita and Copán Ruinas.

source.title: Descubre los útiles escolares en idioma ch'orti'

facts.text: In 2025 the Academy of Mayan Languages of Guatemala translated the national symbols into Ch'orti'; the flag, for example, is tz'apray b'ujk.

source.title: Símbolos patrios en ch'orti: un aporte para preservar el idioma y la identidad

nations.name: Bribri
nations.lands: The Talamanca mountains of southern Costa Rica, on both the Caribbean (Limón) and Pacific (Puntarenas) sides, with smaller communities in Bocas del Toro, Panama

facts.text: The Bribri language is spoken on both sides of Costa Rica's Talamanca mountains, in Limón and Puntarenas, in three regional varieties named for Amubre, Coroma and Salitre.
Bribri communities also live in Panama, where the 2023 census counted 766 Bribri people.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Tz'utujil
nations.lands: The southern shore of Lake Atitlán in Sololá, Guatemala, including Santiago Atitlán and San Pedro La Laguna

facts.text: In Santiago Atitlán, a Tz'utujil traditional authority welcomed Indigenous youth from three countries in 2013 and spoke in Tz'utujil about the role of ancestral authorities.

source.title: Indigenous Mayan Youth Forge International Relationships Based on Community Radio

facts.text: Radio Sembrador, a community station in San Pedro La Laguna on Lake Atitlán, broadcasts news and cultural programs in Tz'utujil and Spanish.

source.title: Profile of A Community Radio Station: Radio Sembrador

nations.name: Ixil
nations.lands: The Ixil region of northern Quiché, Guatemala: Nebaj, Chajul and Cotzal

facts.text: Ixil women weavers of the Q'imb'al initiative, with youth and village ancestral authorities, launched Community Radio Tiichajil Tenam in Nebaj to share Ixil cultural values.

source.title: Radio Tiichajil Tenam Becomes a Reality

facts.text: In 2020 Guatemala's Constitutional Court ruled in favor of the Maya Ixil people of Nebaj, restoring their ownership of the communal land of Ak'ul.

source.title: Pueblos Mayas Ixiles y Ch'orti's recuperan certeza jurídica sobre sus tierras

nations.name: Kaqchikel
nations.lands: Central highlands of Guatemala, including Chimaltenango, Sacatepéquez and parts of Sololá

facts.text: Community Radio Naköj in Santo Domingo Xenacoj, working since 2013, produces programs in Kaqchikel and Spanish for about 7,000 Kaqchikel listeners.

source.title: 2020 Community Media COVID-19 Emergency Grant Partners

facts.text: In 2022 the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples was a member of the Maya Kaqchikel people.

source.title: Historic Win: Inter-American Court of Human Rights Rules in Favor of Indigenous Peoples

nations.name: Kaliña
nations.lands: Coastal Suriname and French Guiana, with related communities in Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil

facts.text: In Suriname the Kari'na (Kaliña) live in many villages with their own village heads, including Christiaankondre and Langamankondre at Galibi in Marowijne district.

source.title: Dorpen en Dorpsbesturen
source.publisher: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)

facts.text: Suriname's Indigenous village leaders say legal recognition of collective rights is an obligation, not a policy choice, and in 2026 urged full implementation of the Kaliña and Lokono judgment.

source.title: VIDS dient resolutie in: Voer Kaliña & Lokono-vonnis uit
source.publisher: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)

nations.name: Nahuat Pipil
nations.lands: Western El Salvador, especially Sonsonate and Ahuachapán departments

facts.text: Izalco is the only municipality in El Salvador with an ancestral Indigenous government, made up of mayordomos and mayordomas.

source.title: Radio Sensunat: Broadcasting to Revitalize the Nahuat Language in El Salvador

facts.text: In Santo Domingo de Guzmán, Nahuat-speaking teachers created Nahuatl cribs where children learn the language, and Radio Sensunat promotes Nahuat Pipil culture.

source.title: Radio Sensunat: Broadcasting to Revitalize the Nahuat Language in El Salvador

nations.name: Wayuu
nations.lands: The Guajira Peninsula, shared by northern Colombia (La Guajira) and northwestern Venezuela (Zulia)

facts.text: Wayuu justice rests on dialogue: respected mediators called Pütchipü'üi, or palabreros, settle disputes between clans through repair and compensation. UNESCO listed this system in 2010.

source.title: Wayuu normative system, applied by the Pütchipü'üi (palabrero)

facts.text: The Wayuu live on the Guajira Peninsula, which spans the border between Colombia and Venezuela.

source.title: Wayuu normative system, applied by the Pütchipü'üi (palabrero)

nations.name: Ngäbe
nations.lands: The Ngäbe-Buglé comarca in western Panama (parts of Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí and Veraguas), nearby lands in Panama, and Ngäbe territories in southern Costa Rica

facts.text: Panama's Law 10 of 1997 created the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca and made its lands the collective property of the comarca, closed to private sale.

source.title: Ley 10 de 7 de marzo de 1997, por la cual se crea la Comarca Ngöbe-Buglé
source.publisher: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 444,878 Ngäbe people.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Guna
nations.lands: Gunayala on Panama's Caribbean coast and islands, plus Madungandí and Wargandí in Panama and communities in northwestern Colombia

facts.text: Gunayala's 49 communities govern themselves together through the Guna General Congress, their highest political and administrative body for land, resources and education.

source.title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government

facts.text: Gunayala runs along Panama's Caribbean coast to the Colombian border, with about 315 km of coastline and over 400 small islands and islets.

source.title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government

nations.name: Emberá
nations.lands: The Emberá-Wounaan comarca and collective lands in Darién and eastern Panama, and the Pacific and Chocó regions of Colombia

facts.text: Panama's Law 22 of 1983 created the Emberá comarca in Darién and named its General Congress the highest traditional decision-making body of the Emberá people.

source.title: Ley 22 de 1983, por la cual se crea la Comarca Emberá de Darién
source.publisher: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

facts.text: Bilingual storybooks in Emberá and Spanish are among the learning materials made for the early education of Emberá children in Panama.

source.title: La educación intercultural bilingüe en Panamá
source.publisher: UNICEF Latin America and the Caribbean

nations.name: Binnizá
nations.lands: The Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico, including Juchitán and Tehuantepec

facts.text: Velas, festivals honoring patron saints, family names, trades and places, are a central Binnizá institution; Juchitán alone celebrates about 24 of them.

source.title: Zapotecos (del Istmo, Valles centrales y Sierra Norte) : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Tutunakú
nations.lands: The Totonacapan: northern Veracruz around Papantla and the Sierra Norte de Puebla, Mexico

facts.text: Community groups asked for radio in their own languages, and since 1994 La Voz de la Sierra Norte in Cuetzalan, Puebla has served Nahua and Totonac peoples.

source.title: XECTZ La Voz de la Sierra Norte (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: At the Centre for Indigenous Arts, Totonac is the language of teaching, and each art is taught in its own house-school, laid out like a traditional settlement.

source.title: Xtaxkgakget Makgkaxtlawana: the Centre for Indigenous Arts and its contribution to safeguarding the intangible cultural heritage of the Totonac people of Veracruz, Mexico

nations.name: Ayuuk
nations.lands: The Sierra Mixe of northeastern Oaxaca, Mexico, including Tlahuitoltepec, Tamazulapam, Ayutla and Guichicovi

facts.text: Backstrap loom weaving continues in Tamazulapam, Tlahuitoltepec and Cotzocón, and young Ayuuk artists are taking up mural and canvas painting.

source.title: Mixes : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

facts.text: In the Ayuuk language the word for a festival is xëëw, which also means day, sun, time and name.

source.title: Mixes : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Maya
nations.lands: Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo, on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula

facts.text: La Voz de los Mayas, an INPI radio station broadcasting from Peto, Yucatán since 1982, reaches 677 localities across the peninsula in Maya and Spanish.

source.title: XEPET La Voz de los Mayas (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI
